item.title: Tamba-yaki: 800 Years of Unglazed Stoneware — Guide
item.description: Tamba-yaki is one of the Six Ancient Kilns of Japan, the handful of pottery centres that have fired continuously since the medieval period, and its kilns have been working in the hills of Tamba-Sasayama for roughly 800 years. The style is defined by what it refuses to add: no applied glaze, the surfaces instead coloured by wood ash falling on the clay in long climbing-kiln firings, producing greens, browns and glassy runs no two of which are alike.

item.title: Nishijin Textile Guide: Kyoto's Ancient Silk-Weaving District
item.description: For over a thousand years, the looms of Kyoto’s Nishijin district have produced Japan’s most luxurious woven silk — the gorgeous, intricately patterned Nishijin-ori fabric used for the finest kimono and obi. Walk these quiet northwest Kyoto backstreets and you can still hear the clatter of looms in workshops handed down through generations. For visitors, Nishijin offers a chance to watch master weavers at work, see dazzling kimono shows, try weaving yourself, and understand the craft behind the kimono you see all over the city.

item.title: Ryukyu Glass Guide: Glass-Blowing Workshops & Shopping
item.description: Ryukyu glass is one of Okinawa’s most colourful crafts — thick, vivid glassware flecked with playful bubbles, born after WWII when artisans recycled discarded American bottles into beautiful new forms. Today the tradition thrives, and visitors can do more than shop: at studios across the island you can blow your own glass — a cup or small piece in the colours of the Okinawan sea and sky. Hands-on, beginner-friendly and rewarding, it’s one of the most popular craft experiences in Okinawa.

item.title: Ryukyu Mura Guide: Tickets, Eisa Shows & Access
item.description: Ryukyu Mura is an open-air theme park in Onna, central Okinawa, that recreates the look and life of an old Ryukyu Kingdom village. Relocated traditional houses with red-tiled roofs and guardian shisa, costumed staff, lively eisa drum-and-dance performances, sanshin music and hands-on craft workshops make it an easy, family-friendly introduction to Okinawan culture. It’s a popular stop on the way up the west coast toward the Churaumi Aquarium. This guide covers the village, performances, craft experiences, tickets and how to get there.

item.title: Yachimun Pottery Guide: Tsuboya Street & Workshops (Naha)
item.description: Yachimun is the Okinawan word for pottery, and the island’s bold, earthy ceramics are among its most beloved crafts. The heart of the tradition is Tsuboya, a historic pottery quarter just off Kokusai-dori in Naha, where a charming stone-paved lane is lined with kilns, studios, galleries and shops. Here you’ll find rustic plates and cups, awamori flasks, and the famous shisa lion-dog guardians. Browsing the lane — or trying the wheel yourself — is a lovely, low-key cultural break in the city.

item.title: Iwate Girls' Trip: Morioka Cafes, Nanbu Crafts & Hot Spring Retreats
item.description: Girls' Group Travel Guide to Iwate Prefecture Iwate Prefecture, stretching across northern Honshu, offers the perfect blend of cultural craftsmanship, cozy café culture, and restorative onsen experiences that make for an unforgettable girls' getaway. Away from the crowds of more tourist-heavy destinations, Iwate welcomes visitors with genuine warmth, artisan traditions, and Instagram-worthy moments around every corner. 1. Morioka’s Coffee & Café Culture Morioka has earned a reputation as one of Japan’s most charming café cities, with the highest number of coffee shops per capita in the country.

item.title: Iwate Leisure: Cycling, Folklore, Craft Workshops & Coastal Activities
item.description: Leisure Activities Guide to Iwate Prefecture Iwate Prefecture, located in northern Honshu’s Tohoku region, offers international visitors an authentic Japanese experience far from the crowded tourist circuits. From UNESCO World Heritage sites to folklore villages and coastal adventures, Iwate combines cultural depth with natural beauty. This guide explores the prefecture’s most rewarding leisure activities. 1. Exploring Hiraizumi by Bicycle Hiraizumi, a compact town housing UNESCO World Heritage sites from the 12th-century Northern Fujiwara clan, is ideally explored by bicycle.

item.title: Nara Girls' Trip: Naramachi Shopping, Deer Selfies & Traditional Craft Experiences
item.description: Nara is an ideal girls' trip destination — compact enough to cover in two days, rich in photogenic moments, and offering craft and food experiences that are genuinely hands-on rather than purely observational. The combination of the deer park (endlessly photogenic, socially energising), Naramachi’s machiya shopping streets (indie boutiques, sweets, calligraphy supplies), and the surrounding craft workshops makes Nara one of the most satisfying Japanese city breaks for a small group of friends.

item.title: Nara Leisure: Ink-making, Calligraphy, Deer Park Experiences & Cultural Crafts
item.description: Nara offers something increasingly rare in Japanese tourism: hands-on connection with living craft traditions that have continued in the same location for centuries. The city and its surrounding region have been producing Japan’s finest ink since the 8th century, brewing sake since mythological times, and working cedar wood in Yoshino since the ancient timber trade. The experiences below go beyond tourist-demonstration level — several connect you with workshops and producers who supply professional artists, monks, and architects throughout Japan.

item.title: Kanazawa Crafts: Gold Leaf, Kutani Pottery, Kaga Yuzen & Wajima Lacquer
item.description: Kanazawa’s extraordinary concentration of traditional crafts is not accidental. The Maeda lords who ruled Kaga Domain for three centuries were deliberate patrons of craft culture, importing master artisans from Kyoto and other craft centres to establish and elevate the regional traditions. Unable to spend their wealth on military expansion (the Tokugawa peace made warfare impossible), the Maeda channelled resources into ceramics workshops, silk dyeing studios, and gold leaf production on a scale that made Kanazawa the pre-eminent craft city of Japan outside Kyoto.
